    Expected wins are Nb/L≈333,333.33Nb/L \approx 333{,}333.33Nb/L≈333,333.33, giving 300,000 successful impressions, 150 attributed conversions, $4,500 of network collections, $2,000 of media spend and a $2,500 gross spread. The bid is higher than the ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1 bid of 6.324555 CPM because the network pays for only 90% of its wins, so the same budget supports a higher price.

    Case B's contract creates a media payment obligation when the auction is won, so the network pays even if display later fails. This is a contract term; it does not license treating the protocol's nurl as billing evidence. Then:

    πB(b)=(ρv−b)F(b),CB(b)=bF(b).\pi_B(b)=(\rho v-b)F(b),\qquad C_B(b)=bF(b).πB​(b)=(ρv−b)F(b),CB​(b)=bF(b).

    The unconstrained optimum drops to b=ρv/2=$0.00675b = \rho v/2 = \$0.00675b=ρv/2=$0.00675 ($6.75 CPM), with expected spend N(ρv/2)2/L=$2,278.125>$2,000N(\rho v/2)^2/L = \$2{,}278.125 > \$2{,}000N(ρv/2)2/L=$2,278.125>$2,000, so the budget binds again. Cost is not scaled by ρ\rhoρ, so the budget-constrained bid is again BL/N≈$0.006324555\sqrt{BL/N} \approx \$0.006324555BL/N​≈$0.006324555 (6.324555 CPM). Expected wins are about 316,227.77, successful impressions about 284,604.99, attributed conversions about 142.302495, network collections about $4,269.07 and gross spread about $2,269.07. The $230.93 shortfall against Case A comes from paying for the 10% of wins that never display, which consumes (1−ρ)B=$200(1-\rho)B = \$200(1−ρ)B=$200 of the budget.

    The contract therefore changes the bid and the returns, not just the event names in reports. If the probability of a successful impression varies with ZZZ, the bid or the quality of the opportunity, you cannot pull a constant ρ\rhoρ out of the expectation; you must model the conditional display probability and the payment function explicitly. On the systems side, the reservation must cover the maximum payment obligation under the contract. In both cases that is bbb per bid: a hard-quota reservation cannot be cut by 10% just because the expected display probability is 90%.

    Division of labor between expected-budget control and hard budgets

    This section switches from expected cost per request to actual ledger quantities, all in dollars for one accounting period. Let CCC be confirmed cumulative media spend (not the per-request expectation CAC_ACA​ or CBC_BCB​ above), RRR the total of maximum possible payment obligations not yet discharged (open reservations), and BBB the hard media budget. RRR here is the reservation total, not the revenue function R(C)R(C)R(C) from Chapter 2. Let cic_ici​ be the cost cap of bid iii (the most it can ever be charged, fees included) and pip_ipi​ its actual billed amount. A hard budget means maintaining the invariant below on every path:

    invariant:C+R≤Badmit bid i only if C+R+ci≤B:R←R+cibill bid i at pi≤ci:C←C+pi,  R←R−ciauthoritative loss or cancellation of i:R←R−ci\begin{aligned} &\text{invariant:} && C+R\le B\\ &\text{admit bid } i \text{ only if } C+R+c_i\le B: && R \leftarrow R+c_i\\ &\text{bill bid } i \text{ at } p_i\le c_i: && C \leftarrow C+p_i,\; R \leftarrow R-c_i\\ &\text{authoritative loss or cancellation of } i: && R \leftarrow R-c_i \end{aligned}​invariant:admit bid i only if C+R+ci​≤B:bill bid i at pi​≤ci​:authoritative loss or cancellation of i:​​C+R≤BR←R+ci​C←C+pi​,R←R−ci​R←R−ci​​

    Billing changes C+RC+RC+R by pi−ci≤0p_i - c_i \le 0pi​−ci​≤0, so only admission can raise it, and admission checks the bound. This holds under three conditions. Every bid has a reliable cap cic_ici​. Each admission is an atomic check-and-reserve: either a serializable update of a single counter, or escrow, where BBB is split into per-node quotas whose sum is provably at most BBB, each node enforces its own quota, and moving quota between nodes is atomic (or the donor debits before the recipient credits). And each billing or release step applies its two updates atomically, exactly once per bid.

    The definitions of cic_ici​ and RRR must cover fees, spend not yet reported, bids whose local timeout expired but that the exchange may still have accepted, and late billing. Reserving expected cost (win probability × bid) instead of cic_ici​ frees capital, but then you have statistical overspend control, not a proof of zero overspend on every path. The overshoot tail depends on correlation between outcomes, and correlated outcomes are exactly what incidents produce. The expiry of a multi-region lease likewise does not discharge obligations already incurred with an external party.

    Keep safety separate from capital availability. Never releasing an undischarged reservation keeps the budget safe but locks up quota. A safe release needs one of: an authoritative final loss (for example a lurl call, where the contract makes it authoritative), a cancellation, a reconciliation result, or a binding contractual cutoff that extinguishes any remaining payment obligation. Such evidence can arrive early, so release need not wait for a deadline. An empirical upper bound on callback delay, or a local TTL, does not terminate a payment obligation. If no confirmable discharge mechanism exists, the system can either hold the reservation indefinitely or accept statistical overspend within an explicit risk limit; the latter is no longer a per-path hard-budget guarantee.

    In this example, holding the full cap for every bid until the end of the period would starve delivery. Each bid reserves $0.006324555, so the $2,000 budget admits at most 2000/0.006324555≈316,2282000/0.006324555 \approx 316{,}2282000/0.006324555≈316,228 bids before any reservation is released, about a third of the 1,000,000 requests. At the same bid and a 31.6% win rate, those yield about 100,000 wins, $632.46 of spend and an $867.54 gross spread, against $2,743.42 when losses are released promptly (Chapter 3, ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1). So release clearly lost bids promptly, shorten the time to confirm obligations, and allocate quota to regions or shards according to supply quality. Conservative reservation lowers overspend risk but causes under-delivery (spending less than planned). Measure that cost as lost gross spread, not as lock contention or budget-service QPS (queries per second).

    A hard cap on the advertiser's CPA bill is a separate problem. Post-click conversions arrive with a delay and still create receivables, so shutting off new media buying cannot stop impressions already delivered from producing further billable events. Handle this with contract terms, conservative control of the remaining quota and explicit tracking of in-flight conversion obligations. Do not pass off the media ledger as the advertiser ledger.

    Correctness boundaries for data and model releases

    Decision logs must link at least: the bid opportunity's identity; candidate eligibility and the final action; the timestamp or version of the features that were available; predicted probabilities and valuations; bid and budget policy; experiment assignment; win, loss and rejection reasons; impression, click and conversion times; attribution rules; billing status; and later adjustments. Not every field can be kept forever, and access and retention policies must match data permissions.

    Training samples must be reproducible at a specific version. Track the model, the calibrator (the post-hoc map from raw model score to probability), feature definitions, creatives and budget-control parameters together. Train only on matured labels, i.e. examples whose attribution window has closed, so that a missing conversion really is a negative. If one release changes both the model and the attribution window, you cannot tell why online results moved, even if they improved. Rolling back the model without rolling back features or the calibrator may not restore the old behavior either.

    A shadow deployment (the new model scores live traffic, but its outputs drive no decisions) can expose latency and distribution anomalies. Because it does not affect which opportunities are bought, it cannot show that the model makes money online. After a canary rollout (the new model controls a small share of live traffic), check whether the traffic mix and price distribution changed, and evaluate under the same budget constraints with matured labels. A new policy buying different opportunities is part of its effect. You cannot take credit for its traffic selection while analyzing the two arms as if they had bought the same samples.

    A dashboard that drives action

    Good monitoring ties each failure to an economic consequence. On-time response rate and no-bid rate broken down by reason explain lost opportunities. The gap between wins and billable impressions explains delivery and integration risk. The amount and age of open obligations explain budget lock-up. Duplicate billing, settlement discrepancies and the overspend tail measure financial correctness. Per-segment calibration, matured CPA and ROAS (attributed revenue divided by ad spend; Chapter 2) and incremental contribution (Chapter 4) measure policy quality.

    Signal Investigate first Conclusions you cannot draw directly
    Win rate up while profit down Bids, competing prices, traffic mix, fees The model is definitely worse, or definitely better
    Clicks up while conversions down Creatives, landing pages, click authenticity, label maturity CTR (click-through rate) should get more weight
    Sudden drop in spend Eligibility, deadlines, quota, economic constraints All under-delivery is a pacing failure
    Sudden drop in reported CPA Windows, attribution rules, event deduplication, backfill The customer got an equally large incremental lift
    Offline gain, online decline Time leakage, calibration, traffic selection, latency, release versions Just switch to a bigger model

    Thresholds come from contracts, loss tolerance and business objectives; there is no industry-standard number to copy. Duplicate billing, budget violations and changes to value definitions should each be able to trigger a stop-loss on its own. You cannot wait for conversion reports days later to discover that today's system is already out of control.

    AppLovin and Axon

    This chapter sorts claims into three bins and labels each one. Public fact: stated in an SEC filing or in AppLovin's own documentation (a company statement, not an independent audit). Inference: our reasoning from those facts. Unknown: not determinable from public sources. All pages were retrieved on November 11, 2026.

    What public sources confirm about the products

    Vocabulary first. AppLovin is the ad-tech company under discussion (Chapter 1). A publisher is an app developer that sells ad slots inside its app; an advertiser buys them; an impression is one ad display. An SDK (software development kit) is a library compiled into the app; ad networks reach in-app inventory through SDKs. Mediation software sits in the publisher's app and decides, for each ad request, which of many demand sources fills it (Chapter 2). Under a waterfall, mediation calls ad networks one after another in a configured priority order; under in-app bidding, networks submit real-time bids for the same request and the highest bid wins. MAX is AppLovin's mediation product, which the company calls its in-app bidding solution. Axon is AppLovin's ad prediction and bidding engine; Axon Ads Manager is the advertiser-facing product it powers.

    Public fact. AppLovin describes Axon as an AI advertising engine whose predictive models evaluate potential impressions. AppLovin then bids on each impression according to the value Axon assigns to it for a given advertiser, aiming at that advertiser's return-on-ad-spend (ROAS) goal. The 2025 Form 10-K says Axon Ads Manager generates substantially all of AppLovin's revenue. Axon official description, AppLovin 2025 10-K

    Public fact. MAX's partner documentation describes a unified first-price auction. The MAX auction server merges real-time bids with the non-bidding networks in the publisher's waterfall. After the auction, the app loads the winning ad. If the load succeeds, MAX sends the winner a win notice; if it fails, MAX sends a loss notice. MAX calls the winner's billing URL only after the ad renders. MAX auction flow

    Do not generalize this sequence. It is MAX's interface semantics. OpenRTB, the IAB Tech Lab's real-time bidding protocol, has analogous win and billing callbacks (nurl, burl), but each exchange decides when they fire and what they commit the buyer to (Chapter 5). MAX's choices do not redefine those terms for other OpenRTB integrations.

    Public fact. The 10-K states that AppLovin is an agent, not a principal, in its advertising arrangements: it does not control the inventory before it passes to the advertiser and is not primarily responsible for delivering it. Under US GAAP an agent reports revenue net, so reported revenue is advertiser payments minus amounts paid or payable to publishers. Revenue is recognized when an impression is delivered (impression-based arrangements) or when a specified action such as a click or install occurs (action-based arrangements). The price itself is set dynamically from the advertiser's campaign goals, not as a fixed price per impression or per action. Revenue recognition note, AppLovin 2025 10-K

    Inference. Because revenue is net, you cannot recover total advertiser spend, and therefore cannot compute the platform's take rate (amount retained as a share of advertiser spend, Chapter 2), from reported revenue alone. Likewise, "MAX mediation is free for publishers" on the MAX website does not mean MAX is free to everyone in the chain. The same FAQ says bidding networks pay AppLovin a fee on the ad revenue they generate, and the 10-K says MAX revenue is "a percentage of client spend." MAX website FAQ, AppLovin 2025 10-K

    Seeing data is not the same as being allowed to train on it

    Public fact (company statement). AppLovin's Axon page lists the inputs it says Axon uses: device and network information; engagement data about apps, ads and other digital properties, collected by AppLovin or shared by partners; advertisers' own user data, if they choose to share it; and win/loss notices from MAX, which every bidder receives for the impressions it bid on. The page also says AppLovin does not collect, and its models do not ingest, other bidders' bid information or other bidders' user data. Axon data description

    Public fact. Adjust is AppLovin's MMP (mobile measurement partner): a third party that advertisers use to attribute installs and in-app events to the ads that drove them (Chapter 2, Chapter 4). The 10-K says Adjust is operated by a wholly owned subsidiary and that data generated by Adjust's services is not shared with AppLovin or used to optimize its recommendation engine (the 10-K's term for Axon) unless a customer directs it. Separately, AppLovin sold its Apps business, its own portfolio of mobile games, to Tripledot; the sale closed on June 30, 2025. AppLovin 2025 10-K

    These are the company's own statements and disclosures. Nobody outside the company has audited the data pipeline in public.

    Inference. The phrase "data flywheel" bundles four separate propositions. Each has a different evidentiary status:

    PropositionStatusWhat public sources say
    MAX receives every bid in order to run the auction.Public factFollows from the documented unified auction: the auction server must see the bids to rank them.
    Axon is permitted to use those bids.Company deniesThe Axon page says the models do not ingest other bidders' bid information or user data. Only win/loss notices, which all bidders receive, are listed as inputs.
    The training pipeline actually uses them.UnknownNo public audit either way.
    Only AppLovin has this data.UnknownNot established. Win/loss notices go to every bidder, and Adjust data is excluded by default.

    Owning a measurement company does not mean owning all of its customers' data for training. Merging the four propositions into one "flywheel" assumes the competitive advantage that the argument is supposed to prove.

    Unknown. Public materials do not reveal Axon's current model architecture, parameter count, feature coverage, training frequency, loss function or budget controller. Nor can they separate how much of a given quarter's growth came from the model, the creatives, supply access, customer mix or attribution rules. The architecture diagrams and algorithms elsewhere in this reader are tools for understanding the problem, not a reverse-engineering of Axon.

    How a prediction advantage becomes retained profit

    Start from a standard result: for a single decision-maker, the optimal value of extra information is nonnegative. Let Π(I)\Pi(\mathcal I)Π(I) be the set of feasible policies (same objective, actions and budget constraints) that are measurable with respect to information I\mathcal II. Then

    Iold⊆Inew  ⇒  Π(Iold)⊆Π(Inew)  ⇒  max⁡π∈Π(Inew)E[u(π)] ≥ max⁡π∈Π(Iold)E[u(π)].\mathcal I_{\text{old}}\subseteq\mathcal I_{\text{new}}\;\Rightarrow\;\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{old}})\subseteq\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{new}})\;\Rightarrow\;\max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{new}})}\mathbb E[u(\pi)]\ \ge\ \max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{old}})}\mathbb E[u(\pi)].Iold​⊆Inew​⇒Π(Iold​)⊆Π(Inew​)⇒π∈Π(Inew​)max​E[u(π)] ≥ π∈Π(Iold​)max​E[u(π)].

    The new decision-maker can always ignore the extra information and replay the old policy. The result needs every one of these premises:

    • Competitors' strategies and the distribution of clearing prices stay fixed.
    • The objective, the action set and constraints such as budget are unchanged.
    • Acquiring and using the information costs nothing.
    • The new information is available at decision time and refines the old (the old signal can be recovered from the new one).
    • Conditional valuations are accurate, and the policy actually optimizes on them.

    A higher offline AUC (ranking quality on held-out logs) establishes none of this. It does not show that the new information set contains the old one, that probabilities are calibrated, or that decisions are optimal. Still less does it show that the gain survives once the market reacts.

    Inference. Suppose a new model finds more valuable opportunities. It can stop buying low-value impressions, and it can bid more for high-value ones. Bidding more raises publisher revenue. Competitors and publishers' floor prices (the minimum price a seller accepts, Chapter 3) keep adjusting, and advertisers may push for better pricing. How the resulting rent is split depends on whether the information is exclusive, whether access to it is stable, whether the model generalizes, whether customers have alternatives, and how the platform charges. Both "a model lead turns entirely into profit" and "auctions compete away every advantage" overstate the case.

    To test for a moat, do not ask whether a competitor can build a similar model. Ask whether, on the same supply surface (the inventory one can bid on), with comparable data permissions, label maturity windows (how long one waits before treating a conversion label as final) and budget constraints, new advertisers and additional budget keep producing incremental contribution. Model, measurement, supply access, creatives, execution cost and customer relationships all have to enter the explanation together. Correct for survivorship bias too: a showcase of the surviving high-return customers proves nothing about the rest.

    Inference (generic, not a claim about AppLovin's practices). If a platform subsidizes advertisers, for example with credits or discounted pricing, the subsidy buys room for trial and error. It does not buy unbiased labels (the conversion and revenue events used as training targets). Suppose labels come only from subsidized customers, cheap traffic or high-intent retargeting (showing ads to users who have already interacted with the advertiser, and who would often convert anyway). Then the learned relationships may not transfer to the broader market once full pricing applies. The early metrics to check are customer retention after subsidies end, the quality of matured labels the platform is permitted to use, calibration within each segment, and the marginal profit curve. Event counts alone say little.

    Three problems that attractive numbers hide

    Definitions for this section. pCTR is the model's predicted click probability for an impression. Clearing CPM is 1,000 × media cost / impressions: what the buyer actually paid, per thousand impressions. Publisher eCPM is 1,000 × publisher revenue / impressions. A cohort is the set of users acquired by a campaign in a given period. Attributed revenue is revenue that the attribution rule credits to the ad; it is not the same as incremental revenue, the revenue that would not have occurred without the ad (Chapter 4). For a cohort CCC with acquisition spend SCS_CSC​, where user uuu was acquired at time tut_utu​,

    D7 ROAS(C)=∑u∈CRu([tu,  tu+168 h))SC,\text{D7 ROAS}(C)=\frac{\sum_{u\in C}R_u\big([t_u,\;t_u+168\,\text{h})\big)}{S_C},D7 ROAS(C)=SC​∑u∈C​Ru​([tu​,tu​+168h))​,

    where Ru(⋅)R_u(\cdot)Ru​(⋅) is attributed revenue from user uuu in the half-open window. Compute it only after every user's 7-day window has fully elapsed. It remains an attributed return, not an incremental one.

    1. Higher pCTR with flat ROAS. If pCTR rises, clearing CPM rises with it and D7 ROAS stays flat, the model may simply be buying more clickable traffic at a higher price. Decompose the change into price and traffic mix before declaring a win on pCTR or offline AUC.
    2. Higher publisher eCPM. If MAX publisher eCPM rises, publishers earn more per thousand impressions. Total publisher revenue also depends on impression volume. Neither number shows that advertisers gained matching incremental profit; higher prices can mean the opposite.
    3. Subsidized growth. If subsidies bring in more advertisers and conversions, but retention falls once full pricing applies, the subsidy may have bought a training distribution that cannot be reproduced.

    For a would-be entrant, technical replicability is only one dimension. The questions that need evidence are: which labels you are permitted to obtain, which supply you can access, how you identify each customer's incrementality, under what constraints marginal returns stay positive, and how long those conditions last.

    Comprehensive exercises and answers

    Ten questions, 100 points

    Shared parameters for Questions 2–4. These are the numbers of the running campaign introduced in “A fictional campaign used throughout” (A one-day learning roadmap) and worked through in From prediction to bidding and budgets.

    • Opportunities. N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 statistically identical bid opportunities (bid requests from publishers). Every auction win yields exactly one successful impression; display failures are ignored here (Real-time advertising systems relaxes this).
    • Contracts. The ad network sells to the advertiser on CPA terms: it charges $30 per billable attributed conversion, i.e. a conversion that the agreed attribution rules credit to the ad and that the contract makes payable. It buys impressions from publishers in first-price auctions: the winner pays its own bid, per impression.
    • Conversion probability. Each impression produces a billable attributed conversion with probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005, the same for every opportunity and independent of the bid and of competition. The network's expected collections per impression are therefore v=30q=0.015v=30q=0.015v=30q=0.015 dollars.
    • Advertiser economics. Pre-advertising contribution per order is g=40g=40g=40 dollars: sales revenue minus goods, fulfillment and other per-order variable costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. The true causal lift is Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002: for the same opportunity, showing the ad raises the probability of an order by 0.0002 compared with not showing it. Attributed conversions are not all caused by the ad, so Δq<q\Delta q<qΔq<q.
    • Competition. The competitive threshold ZZZ is the highest competing bid for an opportunity, in dollars per impression. Assume Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L) with L=0.02L=0.02L=0.02, independently across opportunities. A bid bbb wins when b≥Zb\ge Zb≥Z, so the win rate is F(b)=b/LF(b)=b/LF(b)=b/L for 0≤b≤L0\le b\le L0≤b≤L.
    • Objective. Unless a question says otherwise, the network picks one uniform bid bbb for all opportunities to maximize expected media gross spread: expected collections from the advertiser minus expected payments to publishers. There is no budget, except in Question 4, which adds a media budget B=2,000B=2{,}000B=2,000 dollars on expected media cost over the NNN opportunities.
    • Units. “Spend”, “bill” and “collections” mean expected values. CPM is a price per thousand impressions; eCPM (effective CPM) expresses any expected amount per impression as an amount per thousand impressions. Convert dollars per impression to CPM by multiplying by 1,000.

    Each question is worth 10 points. Spend 30 minutes answering on your own, then 20 minutes checking against the answers. Calculation questions are graded on the numbers and on whether you name the right party, units and assumptions. A score of at least 80, with no conceptual errors on Questions 2, 6 and 8, means you have a working framework for discussing and reviewing ad systems. This is this reader's own pass mark, not an industry certification.

    Question 1: Product dimensions. An ad runs in a mobile game's rewarded video slot (a video the player chooses to watch in exchange for an in-game reward), and the impression is bought in a real-time auction. The publisher charges the buyer per impression. The advertiser has set a target CPA (tCPA) of $30, the average cost per conversion the bidding algorithm aims for (Products and cash flow). Can you conclude that the advertiser pays only when a conversion happens? Which two kinds of contract information are missing?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 1. No. A target CPA is an optimization target, not a billing unit. An advertiser can be billed per impression or per click while the bidder steers toward an average of $30 per conversion. The two missing kinds of information are:

    1. The advertiser-side billing basis: is the advertiser billed per impression, click, install or conversion, and at what price?
    2. The definition of a billable conversion: which event counts, the attribution window, deduplication rules, and refund and chargeback rules.

    The publisher-side terms in the question (an auction, priced per impression) say nothing about the advertiser side; the two are separate contracts. Each side's budget must also be confirmed separately and cannot be inferred from the target CPA. Scoring: 5 points for separating the optimization target from the billing basis, 5 points for clearly naming both kinds of missing information.

    Question 2: Three values. Using the shared parameters above, compute three values, each as an eCPM: (a) the network's expected collections; (b) the advertiser's attributed contribution, i.e. attributed conversions valued at ggg each; (c) the advertiser's incremental contribution, i.e. caused orders valued at ggg each. Why can't the network simply replace its own receivables estimate with the advertiser's incremental contribution?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 2.

    (a) network collections=1000⋅q⋅30=1000×0.015=$15 eCPM(b) attributed contribution=1000⋅q⋅g=1000×0.0005×40=$20 eCPM(c) incremental contribution=1000⋅Δq⋅g=1000×0.0002×40=$8 eCPM\begin{aligned} \text{(a) network collections} &= 1000\cdot q\cdot 30 = 1000\times 0.015 = \$15\ \text{eCPM}\\ \text{(b) attributed contribution} &= 1000\cdot q\cdot g = 1000\times 0.0005\times 40 = \$20\ \text{eCPM}\\ \text{(c) incremental contribution} &= 1000\cdot \Delta q\cdot g = 1000\times 0.0002\times 40 = \$8\ \text{eCPM} \end{aligned}(a) network collections(b) attributed contribution(c) incremental contribution​=1000⋅q⋅30=1000×0.015=$15 eCPM=1000⋅q⋅g=1000×0.0005×40=$20 eCPM=1000⋅Δq⋅g=1000×0.0002×40=$8 eCPM​

    The network's receivables are fixed by the contract: it collects $30 for every billable attributed conversion, whether or not the ad caused it. The advertiser's incremental contribution measures what the ads are really worth to the advertiser, and so its long-run willingness to keep paying. It does not change the probability that a given impression triggers a contractual payment, so substituting it for the receivables estimate would misprice every bid. Note what the numbers imply: the advertiser pays $15 per thousand impressions for $8 of incremental contribution, losing $7 per thousand. That is a churn risk the network should track as a separate metric or constraint, not by rewriting its receivables forecast. Scoring: 2 points for each of the three numbers, 4 points for distinguishing the two objectives.

    Question 3: First-price bidding. With v=0.015v=0.015v=0.015, Z∼Uniform(0,0.02)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,0.02)Z∼Uniform(0,0.02) and no budget, derive the optimal uniform bid, the win rate, and the expected media spend and network collections over N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 requests. Then give one condition under which the rule “bid half the value” fails.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 3. Expected gross spread per request is the margin on a win times the win probability:

    m(b)=(v−b) bL=(0.015−b) b0.02,m′(b)=v−2bL=0  ⇒  b∗=v2=0.0075.\begin{aligned} m(b) &= (v-b)\,\frac{b}{L} = \frac{(0.015-b)\,b}{0.02},\\ m'(b) &= \frac{v-2b}{L}=0 \;\Rightarrow\; b^{*}=\frac{v}{2}=0.0075 . \end{aligned}m(b)m′(b)​=(v−b)Lb​=0.02(0.015−b)b​,=Lv−2b​=0⇒b∗=2v​=0.0075.​

    mmm is concave and b∗≤Lb^{*}\le Lb∗≤L, so this is the maximum: a bid of $7.50 CPM. The win rate is 0.0075/0.02=37.5%0.0075/0.02=37.5\%0.0075/0.02=37.5%, giving 375,000 impressions; media spend is 375,000×0.0075=$2,812.50375{,}000\times 0.0075=\$2{,}812.50375,000×0.0075=$2,812.50, network collections 375,000×0.015=$5,625375{,}000\times 0.015=\$5{,}625375,000×0.015=$5,625, and gross spread $2,812.50.

    “Bid half the value” is specific to a uniform threshold starting at zero, with no other constraints. It fails, for example, when the threshold distribution is not uniform; when a budget binds (Question 4); when there is a floor price (a seller's minimum accepted price) or there are fees on top of the bid; or when value is correlated with the threshold. Even with a uniform distribution it fails if the lower bound aaa is positive (the optimum becomes (v+a)/2(v+a)/2(v+a)/2) or if v/2>Lv/2>Lv/2>L (the bid is capped at LLL). Scoring: derivation 4 points, numbers 4 points, failure condition 2 points.

    Question 4: Whose budget? Add a media budget of $2,000 that caps the network's expected media cost over the NNN opportunities. Find the optimal first-price uniform bid and the advertiser's expected bill. If the advertiser then says it also has a hard budget of $2,000 on its own bill, is that bid still acceptable? Bonus: suppose instead that the advertiser's expected bill is capped at $2,000, while the $2,000 media budget stays in place. Find the optimal uniform bid. Does it guarantee that the actual bill never exceeds $2,000?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 4. Expected media cost is C(b)=N⋅bL⋅b=Nb2/LC(b)=N\cdot\frac{b}{L}\cdot b=Nb^2/LC(b)=N⋅Lb​⋅b=Nb2/L, so the budget requires

    b≤BLN=2000×0.021,000,000≈0.0063246.b\le\sqrt{\frac{BL}{N}}=\sqrt{\frac{2000\times 0.02}{1{,}000{,}000}}\approx 0.0063246 .b≤NBL​​=1,000,0002000×0.02​​≈0.0063246.

    Gross spread increases in bbb up to v/2=0.0075v/2=0.0075v/2=0.0075, which lies above this limit, so the budget binds: b∗=min⁡(v/2, BL/N, L)≈0.0063246b^{*}=\min\bigl(v/2,\ \sqrt{BL/N},\ L\bigr)\approx 0.0063246b∗=min(v/2, BL/N​, L)≈0.0063246, i.e. $6.3246 CPM. The win rate is 31.62%, giving about 316,228 impressions and 158.11 expected attributed conversions. The advertiser's expected bill is about $4,743.42 and the gross spread about $2,743.42.

    A $2,000 hard budget on the advertiser's bill rules this bid out: the expected bill alone is $4,743.42. The media budget limits what the network pays publishers, not what it bills the advertiser. A cap on the advertiser's bill has to be enforced separately on the CPA receivables side, including conversions still to come from impressions already bought. Scoring: calculation 6 points, identifying whose budget each constraint is 4 points.

    Question 4 bonus. The expected bill is A(b)=Nv b/LA(b)=N v\,b/LA(b)=Nvb/L. Requiring A(b)≤2000A(b)\le 2000A(b)≤2000 gives

    b≤2000×0.021,000,000×0.015≈0.0026667.b\le\frac{2000\times 0.02}{1{,}000{,}000\times 0.015}\approx 0.0026667 .b≤1,000,000×0.0152000×0.02​≈0.0026667.

    Gross spread still increases in bbb over this range, and media cost at this bid is far below $2,000, so the optimum is b∗≈0.0026667b^{*}\approx 0.0026667b∗≈0.0026667 ($2.67 CPM). The win rate is 13.33%, about 133,333 impressions and 66.67 expected conversions; media cost is Nb2/L≈$355.56Nb^2/L\approx\$355.56Nb2/L≈$355.56 and gross spread about $1,644.44.

    This satisfies only the expected-value constraint. Conversions are random: treating them as Poisson with mean 66.67, the standard deviation is about 8.2 conversions (about $245), and the bill exceeds $2,000 (67 or more conversions) with probability about 50%. Conversions also arrive with a lag after the impressions are bought. A hard cap therefore needs either an earlier stop that leaves room for conversions still in flight, or a contract term under which conversions beyond the cap are not billed and the network absorbs them. The bonus is not scored.

    Question 5: Calibration and sampling. A conversion model is trained on downsampled data: every positive example is kept, and each negative is kept independently with probability 10%, regardless of its features (Attribution, experiments, and data). Training applies no weight correction, and the model is calibrated on the sampled distribution. For some feature vector it outputs 0.5. What is the true conversion probability? Separately: a new model has a higher AUC than the current one, but its predicted probabilities are about twice the observed conversion rates across the board. Can it go live as is?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 5. With negative retention rate s=0.1s=0.1s=0.1 and sampled-data prediction ps=0.5p_s=0.5ps​=0.5:

    p=s ps1−ps+s ps=0.1×0.51−0.5+0.1×0.5=111≈0.0909.p=\frac{s\,p_s}{1-p_s+s\,p_s}=\frac{0.1\times 0.5}{1-0.5+0.1\times 0.5}=\frac{1}{11}\approx 0.0909 .p=1−ps​+sps​sps​​=1−0.5+0.1×0.50.1×0.5​=111​≈0.0909.

    Equivalently, downsampling negatives multiplies the odds by 1/s1/s1/s, so the true odds are 0.1×1=0.10.1\times 1=0.10.1×1=0.1.

    No, it cannot go live as is. AUC depends only on ranking and is unchanged by any monotone transformation of the scores, so it says nothing about calibration. Bids depend on the absolute probability: v=30qv=30qv=30q, so doubling qqq doubles the value the bidder thinks it is buying. In the shared example without a budget, the bid would rise from $7.50 to $15 CPM, where the true expected gross spread (0.015−b) b/L(0.015-b)\,b/L(0.015−b)b/L is zero. Before launch, check that the sampling correction was applied, recalibrate on matured labels, check calibration by segment (a uniform factor of 2 rarely holds everywhere), evaluate the monetary loss rather than ranking metrics, confirm the labels have matured, and then run a limited online experiment. Scoring: number 4 points, calibration and launch logic 6 points.

    Question 6: Incremental profit. This is the experiment from Attribution, experiments, and data. An eligible population is randomly split into a treatment group (the campaign may deliver) and a control group (it may not), 100,000 users each. Over the same matured window, treatment has 1,200 purchases and control 1,000. The attribution system credits 500 of the treatment purchases to the ad. Ad spend is $5,000. Net revenue per purchase is $50 (sales revenue after refunds and other adjustments, before goods, fulfillment and other costs), and the pre-advertising contribution rate is 40% of net revenue. Assume randomization and event definitions are correct and that the groups do not affect each other. Compute attributed ROAS (attributed revenue ÷ ad spend), incremental ROAS (iROAS: incremental revenue ÷ ad spend) and incremental contribution profit (incremental contribution − ad spend). Then explain why you cannot just compare the treatment users who actually saw the ad with the control group.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 6. The groups are the same size, so incremental purchases are 1200−1000=2001200-1000=2001200−1000=200.

    attributed ROAS=500×505000=5iROAS=200×505000=2incremental contribution profit=200×50×0.4−5000=−$1,000\begin{aligned} \text{attributed ROAS} &= \frac{500\times 50}{5000}=5\\ \text{iROAS} &= \frac{200\times 50}{5000}=2\\ \text{incremental contribution profit} &= 200\times 50\times 0.4-5000=-\$1{,}000 \end{aligned}attributed ROASiROASincremental contribution profit​=5000500×50​=5=5000200×50​=2=200×50×0.4−5000=−$1,000​

    Break-even requires an iROAS of 1/0.4=2.51/0.4=2.51/0.4=2.5, so a 5× attributed ROAS coexists with a loss. These are point estimates. If each user buys at most once and users are independent, the standard error of the purchase difference is 1200(1−0.012)+1000(1−0.010)≈46.6\sqrt{1200(1-0.012)+1000(1-0.010)}\approx 46.61200(1−0.012)+1000(1−0.010)​≈46.6, so an approximate 95% interval for incremental purchases is 109 to 291. Each incremental purchase is worth $50×0.4=$20\$50\times0.4=\$20$50×0.4=$20 of contribution, so profit =20⋅lift−5,000=20\cdot\text{lift}-5{,}000=20⋅lift−5,000 lies between about −$2,830 and +$830 (the same calculation as in chapter 4). The lift is clearly positive, but this sample does not settle the sign of the profit.

    Who actually sees the ad is decided after randomization, by targeting, auction wins and how active each user is, and all of these correlate with the propensity to buy. Comparing exposed treatment users with the whole control group compares two populations that are no longer alike, which reintroduces selection bias. Analyze the ITT (intent to treat: the effect by original random assignment) first. Estimating the effect on exposed users needs extra assumptions or designs, for example dividing the ITT by the exposure rate (assuming no effect on unexposed users) or ghost ads that record which control users would have been exposed. Scoring: numbers 6 points, causal and statistical caveats 4 points.

    Question 7: Price feedback. In a first-price auction you bid $8 CPM, win, and pay $8 CPM. Can you use $8 as a supervised label for that auction's competitive threshold ZZZ (From prediction to bidding and budgets)? In a second-price auction, where the winner pays ZZZ, what bias results if you fit a model of ZZZ only on the prices you paid in auctions you won?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 7. No. In first price you pay your own bid, so a win tells you only that Z≤8Z\le 8Z≤8: a censored observation that bounds ZZZ from above, not a label. A loss tells you Z>bZ>bZ>b. You learn more only if the exchange returns an extra signal, such as the minimum bid that would have won.

    In second price, a win reveals ZZZ exactly, but only when Z≤bZ\le bZ≤b. Training on wins alone drops every auction with Z>bZ>bZ>b, so the sample is truncated from above. The fitted distribution of ZZZ is biased low: it underestimates the threshold, overestimates the win rate at any given bid, and understates the cost of winning. The bias is worst on contested, high-value inventory where you lose most often. The fix is to keep the losses as censored observations at bbb and use a censored likelihood (each win contributes the density at ZZZ, each loss 1−F(b)1-F(b)1−F(b)) or a survival-analysis estimator. Scoring: 5 points per part.

    Question 8: Ledger states. A bid is placed under Case A in “How delivery probability changes the bid” (Real-time advertising systems): the publisher is paid only after a successful impression, and the contract names the OpenRTB billing notice burl as the signal that confirms billing. Before the bid was sent, the budget system reserved the bid's maximum possible cost. After the bid, a win notice (nurl) arrives but no billing notice; then a duplicate of the same win notice arrives. Can the system book this as confirmed media spend? Can it release the whole reservation? How should it handle the billing notice when it later arrives twice?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 8.

    • Confirm spend? No. Under this contract, winning the auction does not create a payment obligation; only a successful impression does, and burl is what confirms it. The duplicate win notice is deduplicated on the bid's business key (exchange, request, impression and bid IDs) and changes nothing.
    • Release the whole reservation? No. The impression may still render and the billing notice may arrive late, so the external obligation is still open. Releasing the reservation would let the same budget be spent twice. It may be released only on authoritative evidence that the obligation is gone: a confirmed loss or cancellation, a reconciliation result, or a binding contractual cutoff. A local timeout is not such evidence.
    • Duplicate billing notice. The first valid burl converts the actual billed amount from reserved to confirmed spend and releases any difference between the reservation cap and that amount. The duplicate is an idempotent no-op on the ledger and is logged for reconciliation. Late, missing or mismatched notices go to a pending-reconciliation state and are settled against the exchange's settlement reports. An amount above the reservation cap means the cost-cap premise has broken and goes to exception handling.

    Scoring: distinguishing the states 4 points, managing the open obligation 3 points, idempotency and reconciliation 3 points.

    Question 9: Offline versus online. A new conversion model beats the current one on offline log loss, but in an online A/B test the network's media gross spread (collections minus media cost, From prediction to bidding and budgets) falls. Give four distinct diagnostic hypotheses, and for two of them name the logs or metrics that would confirm or rule them out.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 9. Candidate mechanisms include:

    1. Miscalibration where it matters: average log loss improves while calibration on high-bid traffic worsens, causing overbidding. In first price you win precisely where you overestimate.
    2. Price or traffic-mix shift: offline evaluation uses traffic selected by the old model; the new model bids differently and wins traffic and prices the evaluation set never covered.
    3. Label problems: label delay (immature conversions in the offline set) or leakage (features carrying post-impression information) inflate the offline score.
    4. Training–serving skew: mismatched feature and model versions or features missing online; higher latency causing more timeouts.
    5. Downstream interactions: bid shading, pacing or budget control tuned to the old score distribution, including budget-control oscillation.
    6. Measurement changes: different fees or attribution definitions between the arms.

    Evidence for two of them. Calibration: predicted versus matured realized conversion rates, sliced by arm, publisher and predicted-score bucket. Overbidding and traffic selection: per-arm logs of bids, win rate, clearing price, traffic composition, cost per impression and collections per impression. Scoring: four distinct mechanisms 6 points in total, two pieces of evidence that would actually localize the problem 4 points in total.

    Question 10: Evidence for a moat. MAX is AppLovin's mediation product, which runs publishers' auctions across demand sources; Adjust is its MMP (mobile measurement partner), which attributes conversions on behalf of advertisers; Axon is its prediction and bidding engine (AppLovin and Axon). Someone claims: “MAX sees all bids and Adjust has all the attribution data, so Axon necessarily trains on all of it, and a competitor that can replicate the technology only needs to subsidize data purchases to catch up.” Identify at least four missing links in this argument, and propose one validation metric better than total conversion volume.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Question 10. Missing links:

    1. Data a system sees is not necessarily data it may train on: MAX receives bids in order to run auctions, and contracts and privacy rules govern other uses. MAX also sees only the auctions it mediates, not all bids.
    2. Data permitted for training does not necessarily enter the training pipeline.
    3. Owning a measurement company is not owning its customers' data: Adjust processes attribution data on advertisers' behalf.
    4. More samples are not automatically unbiased or transferable: data collected under one delivery policy and one supply mix is selection-biased.
    5. The same model does not mean the same supply access and execution conditions.
    6. Predicting short-term responses well is not delivering incremental profit to advertisers.
    7. Subsidies cannot show that advertisers stay once full pricing starts.

    Better metrics: advertiser retention and spend after subsidies end; matured incremental contribution (from holdout tests) under the same budget constraint; or the marginal-return curve of additional budget. Scoring: four gaps 8 points, a suitable metric 2 points.

    Sources, errata, and glossary

    An erratum in the RTB monograph’s second-price example

    The monograph “Display Advertising with Real-Time Bidding (RTB) and Behavioural Targeting” (arXiv v2: 122 pages, version dated July 15, 2017; the PDF title page says July 18) is a sound end-to-end account of RTB. One worked example in Section 5.3.4, however, gets its budget equation wrong: it counts the win probability twice. This section re-derives the example and quantifies the error. arXiv metadata

    Symbols

    Notation follows the “Prediction and bidding” chapter. Where the monograph uses a different symbol, it is given in brackets.

    • ZZZ: the competitive threshold, the highest competing bid for one bid request. We win if our bid is at least ZZZ [monograph: market price zzz].
    • L>0L>0L>0: the upper bound of ZZZ. We assume Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L) [monograph: lll].
    • b≥0b\ge 0b≥0: our bid for one request. ZZZ, LLL and bbb are all in dollars per impression (multiply by 1,000 for CPM).
    • F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b): the win probability at bid bbb, and f=F′f=F'f=F′ its density [monograph: w(b)w(b)w(b) and pzp_zpz​].
    • 1{Z≤b}\mathbf{1}\{Z\le b\}1{Z≤b}: the win indicator, 1 on a win and 0 on a loss. E[⋅]E[\cdot]E[⋅] is expectation over ZZZ, and also over rrr where an integral over rrr is written.
    • r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1]r∈[0,1]: the predicted click-through rate (pCTR) of the request, i.e. the probability that a won impression is clicked. Here rrr is a probability, not money. (In the SAM paper cited in the “Prediction and bidding” chapter, rrr is the reward per conversion; that chapter renames it aaa.)
    • b(r)b(r)b(r): the bidding function, which maps a request’s pCTR to a bid.
    • NNN: the number of bid requests the campaign receives over its lifetime [monograph: TTT]. BBB: the total media budget in dollars [monograph: BBB].
    • C(b)=E[Z 1{Z≤b}]C(b)=E[Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z\le b\}]C(b)=E[Z1{Z≤b}]: the expected payment per request, counting zero on a loss, as in the “Prediction and bidding” chapter. c(b)c(b)c(b) is the monograph’s cost function; its Eq. 5.5 defines it as the expected payment given a win, c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b]c(b)=E[Z\mid Z\le b]c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b], so C(b)=c(b) F(b)C(b)=c(b)\,F(b)C(b)=c(b)F(b).
    • λ>0\lambda>0λ>0: the Lagrange multiplier on the budget [monograph: λ\lambdaλ]. The objective here counts clicks, so λ\lambdaλ is in clicks per dollar and 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ is in dollars per click.

    Model and correct solution

    Assumptions (the monograph’s special case): an ideal second-price auction, so the winner pays ZZZ, with no floor price, fees or bid increments; every win yields one billable impression; r∼Uniform(0,1)r\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)r∼Uniform(0,1), independent of ZZZ; and a risk-neutral buyer. For 0≤b≤L0\le b\le L0≤b≤L:

    F(b)=bL,c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b]=b2,C(b)=E[Z 1{Z≤b}]=∫0bzL dz=b22L.F(b)=\frac{b}{L},\qquad c(b)=E[Z\mid Z\le b]=\frac{b}{2},\qquad C(b)=E[Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z\le b\}]=\int_0^b \frac{z}{L}\,dz=\frac{b^2}{2L}.F(b)=Lb​,c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b]=2b​,C(b)=E[Z1{Z≤b}]=∫0b​Lz​dz=2Lb2​.

    The objective is to maximize expected clicks subject to expected spend equal to the budget (the monograph’s Eq. 5.11):

    max⁡b(⋅)  N∫01r F(b(r)) drs.t.N∫01C(b(r)) dr=B.\max_{b(\cdot)}\; N\int_0^1 r\,F\bigl(b(r)\bigr)\,dr \quad\text{s.t.}\quad N\int_0^1 C\bigl(b(r)\bigr)\,dr=B.b(⋅)max​N∫01​rF(b(r))drs.t.N∫01​C(b(r))dr=B.

    The Lagrangian separates across rrr. Maximizing rF(b)−λC(b)rF(b)-\lambda C(b)rF(b)−λC(b) pointwise gives the first-order condition (r−λb) f(b)=0(r-\lambda b)\,f(b)=0(r−λb)f(b)=0, so b(r)=r/λb(r)=r/\lambdab(r)=r/λ as long as r/λ≤Lr/\lambda\le Lr/λ≤L. This is the monograph’s Eq. 5.32, and it is the second-price rule b=v/λb=v/\lambdab=v/λ from the “Prediction and bidding” chapter with value v=rv=rv=r measured in clicks. A linear bid is therefore derived here, not assumed. Expected clicks equal N/(3λL)N/(3\lambda L)N/(3λL), which rise as λ\lambdaλ falls, so the budget binds and the equality constraint is justified. Substituting into the constraint:

    N∫01(r/λ)22L dr=N6λ2L=B  ⟹  1λ∗=6LBN,b∗(r)=r6LBN.N\int_0^1 \frac{(r/\lambda)^2}{2L}\,dr=\frac{N}{6\lambda^2L}=B \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{1}{\lambda^*}=\sqrt{\frac{6LB}{N}},\qquad b^*(r)=r\sqrt{\frac{6LB}{N}}.N∫01​2L(r/λ)2​dr=6λ2LN​=B⟹λ∗1​=N6LB​​,b∗(r)=rN6LB​​.

    The closed form holds only when no bid exceeds LLL, i.e. 1/λ∗≤L1/\lambda^*\le L1/λ∗≤L, which is equivalent to B/N≤L/6B/N\le L/6B/N≤L/6. For L/6<B/N<L/2L/6<B/N<L/2L/6<B/N<L/2 the optimal bid is min⁡(r/λ,L)\min(r/\lambda,L)min(r/λ,L), and λ\lambdaλ solves a different budget equation. For B/N≥L/2B/N\ge L/2B/N≥L/2 the budget never binds, because bidding LLL on every request costs E[Z]=L/2E[Z]=L/2E[Z]=L/2 per request.

    Where the monograph goes wrong

    The monograph’s budget constraint (Eqs. 5.11 and 5.33) is N∫c(b(r)) F(b(r)) dr=BN\int c(b(r))\,F(b(r))\,dr=BN∫c(b(r))F(b(r))dr=B. That is correct, because Eq. 5.5 defines ccc as the conditional payment, so cF=CcF=CcF=C. But Eq. 5.35 (PDF page 58) evaluates c(b)c(b)c(b) as ∫0bz/L dz=b2/(2L)\int_0^b z/L\,dz=b^2/(2L)∫0b​z/Ldz=b2/(2L), without dividing by F(b)F(b)F(b). That expression is C(b)C(b)C(b), not c(b)c(b)c(b). Eq. 5.36 (page 59) then multiplies it by F(b)=b/LF(b)=b/LF(b)=b/L again, so the per-request cost becomes b3/(2L2)b^3/(2L^2)b3/(2L2). With b=r/λb=r/\lambdab=r/λ:

    ∫01(r/λ)32L2 dr=18λ3L2=BN  ⟹  λpaper=12(NBL2)1/3,1λpaper=2(L2BN)1/3.\int_0^1\frac{(r/\lambda)^3}{2L^2}\,dr=\frac{1}{8\lambda^3L^2}=\frac{B}{N} \;\Longrightarrow\; \lambda_{\mathrm{paper}}=\frac12\left(\frac{N}{BL^2}\right)^{1/3},\qquad \frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{paper}}}=2\left(\frac{L^2B}{N}\right)^{1/3}.∫01​2L2(r/λ)3​dr=8λ3L21​=NB​⟹λpaper​=21​(BL2N​)1/3,λpaper​1​=2(NL2B​)1/3.

    These are the monograph’s Eqs. 5.37 and 5.38 (subscript “paper” marks the published value). The linear form b=r/λb=r/\lambdab=r/λ is unaffected; only the coefficient is wrong. The monograph’s first-price result in the same section, b(r)=r3LB/Nb(r)=r\sqrt{3LB/N}b(r)=r3LB/N​ (Eq. 5.29), uses the per-request cost bF(b)=b2/LbF(b)=b^2/LbF(b)=b2/L correctly, so the slip is confined to the second-price case. Page with Eq. 5.5, page with Eq. 5.35, page with Eqs. 5.36–5.38

    Size of the error

    At the published coefficient, the true expected spend per request is (1/λpaper)2/(6L)(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{paper}})^2/(6L)(1/λpaper​)2/(6L). Dividing by the budget per request gives the overspend factor

    (1/λpaper)2/(6L)B/N=23(LNB)1/3.\frac{(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{paper}})^2/(6L)}{B/N}=\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{LN}{B}\right)^{1/3}.B/N(1/λpaper​)2/(6L)​=32​(BLN​)1/3.

    The published formula keeps every bid at or below LLL exactly when B/N≤L/8B/N\le L/8B/N≤L/8, and on that whole range the factor is at least 23⋅81/3=43\tfrac23\cdot 8^{1/3}=\tfrac4332​⋅81/3=34​. Wherever the formula applies, it overspends by at least 33%, and the overspend grows as the budget tightens. Boundary effects cannot explain the gap.

    Check with the “Prediction and bidding” chapter’s numbers: L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02 per impression ($20 CPM), N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 requests and B=$2,000B=\$2{,}000B=$2,000, so B/N=$0.002≤L/8=$0.0025B/N=\$0.002\le L/8=\$0.0025B/N=$0.002≤L/8=$0.0025. The correct coefficient is 6×0.02×0.002=$0.015492\sqrt{6\times0.02\times0.002}=\$0.0154926×0.02×0.002​=$0.015492 per click: a request with pCTR rrr gets a bid of r×$15.49r\times\$15.49r×$15.49 CPM, and expected spend is exactly $2,000. The published coefficient is 2(0.022×0.002)1/3=$0.0185662(0.02^2\times0.002)^{1/3}=\$0.0185662(0.022×0.002)1/3=$0.018566 per click, and its true expected spend is $2,872.58, or 1.436 times the budget. With the unitless values L=1L=1L=1, B/N=0.01B/N=0.01B/N=0.01, the coefficients are 0.244949 and 0.430887 and the overspend factor is 3.094. The main text derives its budget results independently and does not reuse this example.

    Where to read next

    For the full RTB picture, read Chapters 2, 3, 5 and 7 of the RTB monograph. For how industrial click prediction defines and calibrates probabilities, read Google’s 2013 click-prediction paper. To build a real integration, work from OpenRTB and your counterparties’ contracts. To judge whether advertising creates value for customers, read the randomized advertising experiments. In every paper, record the explicit assumptions; they matter more than the model names.

    Resource Purpose
    RTB monograph, pinned v2 Main reference for RTB mechanics, auctions, bidding and attribution; see the erratum above
    Optimal Real-Time Bidding Frameworks Discussion Contrasts the true expected second-price cost with using the bid as a cost upper bound
    Google, Ad Click Prediction (2013) Sampling, calibration and other problems of training click models at production scale
    ESMM Joint modeling of impression → click → conversion to reduce selection bias in conversion-rate models
    Delayed-feedback conversion modeling Conversion labels that arrive late, and the trade-off between label completeness and model freshness
    ICML 2023, first-price bidding with budgets Learning to bid under a budget, with guarantees that depend on what feedback the bidder observes
    Statistical Arbitrage Mining (SAM) Risk and optimization for a buyer that sells on CPA and buys on CPM
    Counterfactual risk minimization Logging policies, propensities and offline evaluation of new policies
    Gordon et al., randomized ad experiments at Facebook How far observational ad measurement departs from randomized estimates of causal effect
    OpenRTB 2.6 Response deadlines, price units, request and response objects, and win, billing and loss notices
    Apple ad attribution What privacy-preserving attribution (AdAttributionKit, SKAdNetwork) lets an advertiser observe, and what it hides
    MAX auction dynamics One mediation platform’s concrete first-price auction flow and notice sequence

    Glossary

    This is the reader’s canonical glossary, in alphabetical order. Definitions give the sense used in this reader; individual contracts and platforms may define a term differently, and the contract wins.

    Term Definition
    A/B testA randomized experiment that assigns users (or requests) to treatment or control so that the difference in outcomes estimates a causal effect.
    Ad exchangeA marketplace that receives bid requests from sellers, runs the auction among buyers and sets the clearing price.
    Ad groupThe level below a campaign that carries finer targeting, bids or creative combinations; the hierarchy differs across platforms.
    Ad loadHow many ads are shown per session or per unit of content; raising it trades user retention for short-term revenue.
    Ad networkAn intermediary that aggregates publishers’ inventory and sells it to advertisers, often buying in one pricing unit (e.g. CPM) and selling in another (e.g. CPA) and keeping the spread.
    Ad opportunityOne chance to show one ad to one user in one slot at one moment; also called an impression opportunity.
    Ad requestAn app’s or page’s request for an ad to fill one slot; mediation or an SSP may fan one ad request out into many bid requests.
    Ad serverThe system that selects which ad to show for a request, delivers it and logs the result.
    AdAttributionKitApple’s privacy-preserving attribution framework (iOS 17.4 and later), successor to SKAdNetwork; it reports conversions in delayed, crowd-anonymized postbacks without user-level identifiers.
    ads.txt / app-ads.txtA file the publisher hosts on its own domain listing the ad systems authorized to sell its inventory (app-ads.txt is the app variant).
    AdvertiserThe buyer: the business that pays for impressions, clicks or actions in order to reach users.
    ATTApp Tracking Transparency: Apple’s iOS permission prompt, required before an app tracks a user across other companies’ apps and websites or reads the IDFA.
    AttributionRule-based assignment of credit for a conversion to earlier ad interactions (commonly last-touch); it is an accounting rule, not a causal estimate.
    Attribution windowThe maximum delay between an ad interaction and a conversion for the conversion to be credited; click-through and view-through windows are set separately. Also called a lookback window.
    AxonAppLovin’s ad prediction and bidding engine.
    BidThe price a buyer offers for one opportunity; most interfaces quote it in CPM.
    Bid requestThe message, usually in OpenRTB format, by which a seller invites buyers to bid on one ad opportunity before a response deadline.
    Bid shadingBidding below one’s value in a first-price auction, trading win probability for a lower payment; at an interior optimum b=v−F(b)/f(b)b=v-F(b)/f(b)b=v−F(b)/f(b).
    Billable eventThe event that triggers payment under a given contract: a win, a rendered impression, a click, an install or a qualifying action.
    burlOpenRTB billing notice URL: the exchange calls it when the impression becomes billable under the exchange’s policy.
    CalibrationThe property that predicted probabilities match observed frequencies (among requests with pCTR 2%, about 2% are clicked); bidding needs it because bids multiply value by probability.
    CampaignAn advertiser’s unit of budget, objective, schedule and targeting.
    Censoring (winning prices)Partial observation of the competitive threshold: on a win in a second-price auction it is observed, on a loss we know only that it exceeded our bid, so regression on wins alone is biased.
    Clearing priceThe price the auction winner actually pays.
    Competitive thresholdThe highest competing bid for an opportunity (or the floor, if higher): the bid needed to win, written ZZZ. The RTB monograph calls it the market price.
    ContributionIn this reader, pre-advertising contribution per order: sales revenue minus cost of goods, fulfillment and other variable non-advertising costs.
    ConversionThe advertiser’s target action after an ad, such as an install, purchase or registration.
    CPACost per action: the price paid per agreed conversion; as a metric, spend divided by conversions.
    CPCCost per click: the price paid per click; as a metric, spend divided by clicks.
    CPICost per install: the price paid per attributed app install.
    CPMCost per mille: the price per 1,000 impressions. A $6 CPM bid is $0.006 for one impression; auctions still sell one impression at a time.
    CTR / pCTRClick-through rate: clicks divided by impressions. pCTR is a model’s predicted probability that one impression is clicked.
    CVR / pCVRConversion rate; the denominator (per click, per impression or per install) must be stated. pCVR is the model’s predicted value.
    Deal typesDirect deal (negotiated by hand, fixed price and volume); programmatic guaranteed (fixed price, reserved volume, automated execution); preferred deal (fixed price, first look, no volume commitment); private auction (invitation-only); open auction (any qualified buyer).
    Delayed feedbackConversions arriving hours to days after the impression, so recent training examples carry incomplete labels: a negative may still convert.
    Demand sourceAny buyer that can fill an ad request: an ad network, a DSP or a direct campaign.
    DSPDemand-side platform: software that bids on impressions across exchanges on behalf of advertisers.
    eCPMEffective CPM: revenue or value per 1,000 impressions, whatever the pricing unit (e.g. CPC × CTR × 1,000); it puts bids priced in different units on one scale.
    Fill rateThe share of ad requests that receive an ad.
    First-price auctionAn auction in which the winner pays its own bid.
    Floor priceThe seller’s minimum acceptable price for an opportunity; bids below it lose. Also called a reserve price.
    Ghost adsAn experiment design that logs, for control users, the impressions the campaign would have won, so the effect on users who would actually be exposed can be estimated without placebo ads.
    Gross spreadA term defined in this reader: an ad network’s collections from advertisers minus its media procurement cost.
    Gross vs net revenueRevenue recognition: a platform that controls the service before it reaches the customer (a principal under IFRS 15 and ASC 606) books the full advertiser spend as revenue (gross); an agent books only its fee (net).
    GSPGeneralized second-price auction for several ranked slots, as in search ads: each winner pays roughly the minimum bid needed to keep its position. Bidding one’s value is not an equilibrium in general.
    Guaranteed deliveryA contract that commits the seller to deliver a fixed volume of qualifying impressions, with a remedy for shortfall.
    HoldoutA randomly selected group withheld from ads (or from a campaign or feature) to serve as the control when measuring incrementality.
    IABInteractive Advertising Bureau, the industry body whose Tech Lab publishes OpenRTB, ads.txt and sellers.json.
    IDFAIdentifier for Advertisers: the per-device iOS advertising identifier, readable only after ATT consent.
    ImpressionOne rendered display of an ad. A “successful impression” here means the display event the contract counts actually completed; a won auction can still fail to render.
    IncrementalityThe change in an outcome caused by showing ads, measured against a randomized counterfactual; also called lift. Contrast with attribution.
    InterstitialA full-screen ad shown at a natural break, such as between game levels.
    IPSInverse propensity scoring: an off-policy estimator that reweights each logged reward by π(a∣x)/μ(a∣x)\pi(a\mid x)/\mu(a\mid x)π(a∣x)/μ(a∣x), the ratio of the new policy’s to the logging policy’s action probability.
    iROASIncremental ROAS: revenue caused by the ads (treatment minus control) divided by ad spend.
    ITTIntent-to-treat effect: the average effect of being assigned to treatment, whether or not the user was actually exposed.
    LTVLifetime value: the value a user generates over a stated horizon. State whether it is revenue or contribution, the horizon, the discounting and whether acquisition cost is already subtracted.
    lurlOpenRTB loss notice URL: the exchange calls it when the bid loses, optionally with a loss-reason code.
    MAXAppLovin’s mediation platform for app publishers.
    MediationSoftware in a publisher’s app that decides which of several demand sources fills each ad request, by a bidding auction, a waterfall or both.
    MMPMobile measurement partner (e.g. Adjust, AppsFlyer): a third party whose SDK records installs and in-app events and attributes them to ad networks.
    nurlOpenRTB win notice URL: the exchange calls it when the bid wins. On its own it does not mean the ad rendered or is billable.
    OpenRTBThe IAB Tech Lab protocol for bid requests, bid responses and notices; this reader cites version 2.6.
    PacingOnline control of the spend rate over the budget period, e.g. by adjusting a bid multiplier toward a target spend trajectory; it works alongside, and does not replace, a hard budget cap.
    PostbackA server-to-server message that reports a conversion, and possibly its value, to the ad network or MMP.
    ProgrammaticBuying and selling ad opportunities through automated systems, one opportunity at a time.
    PSAPublic-service ad: a placebo ad shown to control users in older experiment designs; biased when an optimizer chooses who sees ads.
    PublisherThe owner of the app or website whose ad slots are sold.
    Retrieval and rankingThe stages of ad selection: retrieval picks a small candidate set worth scoring; ranking then estimates response probabilities and value for each candidate.
    Rewarded videoA video ad the user opts into in exchange for an in-app reward.
    ROASReturn on ad spend: attributed revenue divided by ad spend. It ignores cost of goods and does not measure incrementality.
    RPMRevenue per 1,000 ad requests (also called request eCPM); if each filled request yields one impression, RPM = fill rate × impression eCPM.
    RTBReal-time bidding: an auction run separately for each ad opportunity while the user’s page or app waits, typically within about 100 ms.
    SDKSoftware development kit: a library embedded in an app, e.g. by an ad network, mediation platform or MMP.
    Second-price auctionAn auction in which the winner pays the highest competing bid, or the floor if higher. “Ideal second-price” in this reader ignores floors, bid increments and fees.
    sellers.json / SupplyChain objectsellers.json is a file each SSP or exchange publishes listing the sellers it pays; the OpenRTB SupplyChain object lists every intermediary a bid request passed through.
    SettlementThe final, contractually checked computation of who owes whom.
    SKAdNetworkApple’s earlier privacy-preserving install-attribution API (SKAN), succeeded by AdAttributionKit.
    SSPSupply-side platform: software that sells a publisher’s inventory to many buyers and exchanges and manages floor prices.
    Statistical arbitrageHere, buying impressions on CPM while selling outcomes on CPA: profitable in expectation, but exposed to conversion, attribution and payment risk.
    Take rateThe platform’s net revenue divided by the gross advertiser spend that flows through it.
    tCPATarget CPA: the average cost per action an advertiser asks the bidder to aim for; a bidding goal, not a billing price.
    TOT / CACETreatment effect on the treated / complier average causal effect: the effect on users actually exposed; with one-sided noncompliance, the ITT divided by the exposure rate in the treatment group.
    tROASTarget ROAS: the return on ad spend an advertiser asks the bidder to aim for; a bidding goal, not a billing contract.
    View-through conversionA conversion credited to an impression that was not clicked; a click-through conversion follows a click.
    WaterfallA mediation method that calls demand sources one at a time in a configured priority order until one fills the request.
    Win rateThe probability of winning at bid bbb, F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b); as a metric, wins divided by bids.

    Review record

    November 11, 2026 (Chinese edition). An independent Claude Opus 5.5 review covered all eight chapters, formulas, tables, exercises and calculator code. It found no arithmetic or derivation errors but flagged gaps: incremental-ROAS labelling, the successful-impression condition, symbol scope, and definitions used before they were given. The editor revised accordingly and, from the source monograph, corrected one misreading in the review: there rrr is the predicted click-through rate, not a monetary value. Derivations were also checked by numerical integration, grid search over the budget-feasible region, and recomputation of every worked example.

    November 12, 2026 (English edition, first pass). Corrections to translation at inline boundaries, the pacing multiplier, the derivative variable, Axon data qualifiers, chapter references and billing units.

    November 12, 2026 (English edition, close-reading revision). Each chapter was re-derived and rewritten by a separate reviewer, then cross-checked by the editor.

    • Math. No numerical errors were found in the original worked examples. Fixed: the validity range of the corrected budget-bid coefficient (B/N≤L/6B/N\le L/6B/N≤L/6, not a condition on TTT); inconsistent rounding between text and calculator; one confidence interval stated two ways (chapters 4 and 7 now use the same binomial standard error). Added: KKT derivation of the calculator bid with its shadow prices, second-order and boundary checks, pacing as projected dual subgradient descent, the first- and second-price censored likelihoods, the sampling correction in odds form, and an uncertainty analysis showing that the chapter 4 experiment establishes a positive lift but not the sign of the profit.
    • Definitions. Every symbol, acronym and ad-domain term is now defined at or before first use in each chapter, or linked to where it is defined. Parameters that were defined only inside collapsed sections are restated where used. The glossary is the canonical reference.
    • Facts (chapter 6). Claims were spot-checked against AppLovin's 2025 10-K and its MAX and Axon documentation: net (agent) revenue recognition with dynamically set prices, the MAX fee on bidding-network revenue, win/loss notices sent to every bidder, and the apps-business sale. Every claim is labelled public fact, inference or unknown.
    • Notation and style. US dollars throughout; one symbol set across chapters 3, 7 and 8 (LLL, NNN, BBB, FFF); all mathematics typeset with KaTeX.

    The review covers the text and code under their stated assumptions. It does not establish that those assumptions hold in any real market. Source page and equation numbers for the RTB monograph were not re-verified in this pass.
